posts.body_html:
You know that scene in Jurassic Park when the peeps were inside their car in the middle of the jungle, and they hear huge footsteps, followed by ripples in the cup of water...... wondering what the heck is out there? Well, that's sorta like the experience my friend Damon and I had in Montgomery...it was midnight and we decided to go find any motel that we could find, so we stopped at the first one we could see off the highway. Right when I pulled in, there were 2 police officers with their lights going and tons of people in the motel standing outside of their door, trying to see what happened. An ambulance had just pulled out and rushed back onto the road. Damon had a very long face, and I innocently told him that I'm going to the office to see if there's a room available. He said, "are you kidding?!" We ended up going across the street to an even sketchier motel, and there were tons of shady looking characters everywhere, walking in the dark in the parking lot! Remeber, it's midnight, what are so many people doing up, walking around? I parked the car right at the entrance of the office, paid for a room, got back into the car, and then drove close to where our room was. We knew there was some sketchy stuff going on out in the dark, but we couldn't see anyone or anything! I told Damon, "okay, here's the plan. grab our luggage as fast as we can, run into our room, and lock the door." The second we opened the door, just like Jurrassic park, random heads came out of nowhere and started rushing towards our us! We quickly grabbed all of our stuff, baller-speed, ran into the motel, shut/locked the door, closed the curtains, and then we were safe! NEVER AGAIN!!!!

Okay, that was Montgomery, Alabama, but every time I look at these seedlings from Montgomery Co, NC, it reminds me of that experience, LOL


So back to the actual plants: I think these originate from a protected site more inland (away from the coast) that is in an unusual hilly habitat, it's not your typical carnivorous plant savanna! The area today is somewhat shaded with tall but sparse trees, although I believe the site is managed and burned. Whatever the case may be, these genetics are very unique, and I do see some signs of historic introgression with S. flava var. flava.

S. purpurea ssp. venosa Montgomery Co, NC, pics tkaen 8/12/21: The parents of this clone or the grandparents could have easily been a catesbaei:


Some individuals almost remind me of the tattnall Co, GA population:


maybe a bit too early to tell what's going on with this clone, almost montana-ey with a weird shape:



great diversity!









These plants have just started putting on some real growth. In the next few weeks, I'll update this thread, should be some more exciting traps to look at, so stay tuned!

It's now starting to become evident how special these genetics are! I think the main feature is the incredible color contrast, along with the diversity of shapes. This population is far from the main venosa populations: it's in a rare hilly habitat that's quite far from the coast, whereas most other venosas originate from a savanna type habitat near the ocean. Pics taken 8/21/21:


I think Even Al Gore would say these are beautiful....er rather GOREgeous?


The hoods on some of these clones fold over the mouth like montanas. This reminds me a lot of the tattnall Co, GA population, which does the same thing:

Aug 23, 2021 13:07:12 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
This population is far from the main venosa populations: it's in a rare hilly habitat that's quite far from the coast, whereas most other montanas originate from a savanna type habitat near the ocean.

hcarlton is trying to orient your sense of direction. The layout in North Carolina is the opposite of that in California: ocean to the east, mountains to the west. You have to go a couple counties to southeast of Montgomery to find the flatter, sandy ground that is more typical venosa habitat (the pine savannas). The var. montana plants grow further west, in the foothills and low mountains of the Appalachians.

A large portion of the Uwharrie Mountains is found in Montgomery County. It's a very old range in the middle of the state. The tallest peak is 1,188 feet / 362 meters, but most of them are just very large hills. I honestly didn't think that any carnivorous plants grew in that area.

I recently bought a couple small divisions of Mike's Montgomery County plants. They have settled in nicely here in eastern North Carolina (close to the I-95 corridor). I'm curious to see how they develop. I currently have 8 Tattnall County plants, including a couple very nice seed-grown ones from Calen Hall. I also have one nice var. montana from Jeremiah Harris (keeping my fingers crossed that this one survives; my two previous montana's didn't enjoy the hot, muggy summers here). It wouldn't surprise me if the Montgomery County plants are an ancestral population of the montana's.

posts.body_html:
If this is the site I'm thinking of, it is protected as one of the few remaining Piedmont bog sites. It also contains S. flava and S. x catesbaei, so neat that you notice it in some traits of these plants! This preserve has some of the few remaining longleaf stands in the piedmont.

There are a few other inland bogs in the Carolinas. Many of these are closer to the sandhills (the hilly region between the low coastal plain and the more elevated piedmont). Some sites contain Atlantic whitecedar streams and look very similar to the Fall Line Sandhill rubra habitat in GA or the gulfensis habitat in FL. The inland Carolina bogs have ssp. rubra, but I think it was Schnell who noted some look similar to jonesii. These whitecedar stream bogs sometimes include purpurea and flava. 

This hilly region is incredibly diverse, but unfortunately almost all destroyed. The Sarracenia we see today is just a limited sample of what used to grow in the region. The reason for the scarcity is due to the relatively rich soil of the piedmont while the fast flowing streams in the Fall Line Sandhills made water mills possible for an early industrializing South. Most of the large cities in the Southeast: Montgomery, Columbus, Macon, Columbia, and Raleigh straddle the fall line. GA has virtually no intact piedmont ecosystems.

It's great that at least couple bogs are preserved and some unique genetics are represented in cultivation.

posts.body_html:
oh wow, nice catesbaei!

Some updated pics, taken 10/19/22. you really can't go wrong with any of these individuals, they're all unique and great looking! Check out the hood on this first one, looks like a montana!


















It was a mistake planting them so close to each other, going to give them more space next grow season. the plants are so packed together, you can't really see each individual, and since they're packed to tightly, the body of the traps receive no light, so they don't color up. If only we could see all of these plants in their fullest glory...next year hopefully!
